program.official_name: New Jersey Earned Income Tax Credit (NJEITC)
program.description: The NJEITC is a cash-back tax credit for working families and individuals, including the self-employed, who earn low to moderate income. For Tax Year 2025 a claimant must have been a New Jersey resident for at least part of the year who works or earns income, must have a qualifying child or be at least 18 years old, must meet the federal income limits for their filing status and claimed dependents, must have a valid Social Security number, and must file a New Jersey Resident Income Tax Return. In general the claimant must also qualify for the federal Earned Income Tax Credit, though New Jersey does not follow the federal age limits. Investment income must be $11,950 or less.
program.plain_language_summary: The NJEITC is money back from the state if you worked and did not earn much. You have to file a New Jersey tax return to get it, even if your income is too low to be required to file. The income limit depends on your filing status and how many children you claim - from $19,104 up to $68,675.
who_it_helps: Working people with low or moderate earnings
Workers aged 18 and over, with or without children

sources.title: Know NJEITC - Eligibility and Earned Income Limits
sources.excerpt:
To be eligible for the NJEITC for Tax Year 2025, you must:
Be a New Jersey resident for at least some of the tax year who works or earns income;
Have a qualifying child and/or be at least 18 years old;
Meet the federal income limits for your filing status and claimed dependents;
Have a valid Social Security number (This includes your spouse and any qualifying dependent you list on your tax return); and
File a New Jersey Resident Income Tax Return (NJ-1040), even if your New Jersey gross income is below the minimum filing threshold amount.
You cannot be listed as a dependent on another tax return.

program.official_name: ANCHOR (Affordable New Jersey Communities for Homeowners and Renters)
program.description: ANCHOR offers property tax relief to New Jersey residents who own or rent their main home in New Jersey and meet the income limits. Homeowners qualify if they owned and occupied a New Jersey home as their principal residence on October 1, 2024, the home was subject to property taxes, and their 2024 New Jersey gross income was not more than $250,000. Renters qualify if they rented and occupied a New Jersey residence as their principal residence on October 1, 2024, their name was on the lease, they paid rent, the property was subject to local property taxes, and their 2024 New Jersey gross income was not more than $150,000. The Division files on behalf of most eligible residents; seniors and recipients of Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability benefits file the combined PAS-1 application.
program.plain_language_summary: ANCHOR is a New Jersey payment that helps with property taxes, and renters get it too. Homeowners can earn up to $250,000 and renters up to $150,000. The state files for most people automatically and sends a confirmation letter, so check whether you already have one before applying.
who_it_helps: Homeowners who paid New Jersey property taxes
Renters whose building pays local property taxes
Seniors and people receiving Social Security disability benefits

sources.title: ANCHOR Program
sources.excerpt:
ANCHOR Homeowner Eligibility Requirements
You are eligible if:
You were a New Jersey resident; and
You owned and occupied a home in New Jersey that was your principal residence (main home) on October 1, 2024; and
Your home was subject to property taxes; and
Your 2024 New Jersey gross income was not more than $250,000.
ANCHOR Renter Eligibility Requirements
You are eligible if:
You were a New Jersey resident; and
You rented and occupied a residence in New Jersey that was your principal residence (main home) on October 1, 2024; and
Your name was on the lease or rental agreement; and
You paid rent; and
The rental property was subject to local property taxes, (see Qualified and Non-Qualified Rental Properties); and
Your 2024 New Jersey gross income was not more than $150,000.

This program offers property tax relief to New Jersey residents who own or rent property in New Jersey as their main home and meet certain income limits. This year's ANCHOR benefit is based on residency, income, and age from 2025.

program.administering_org: New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Division of Unemployment Insurance
program.description: New Jersey Unemployment Insurance pays weekly benefits to workers who lose a job through no fault of their own. Eligibility is based on wage information from employers in the last 18 months, on the reason the claim ended, and on continuing requirements once a claim is open. To qualify on a 2026 claim a worker must have earned at least $310 per week for 20 or more weeks in covered employment during the base year, or at least $15,500 in total. Workers who live in New Jersey but worked only in other states should apply where they physically worked, and self-employed people who do not pay into Unemployment Insurance may not be eligible.
program.plain_language_summary: If you lost your job through no fault of your own, New Jersey Unemployment Insurance pays you every week while you look for work. For a 2026 claim you need to have earned at least $310 a week for 20 weeks, or $15,500 in total, in the year before you apply. You also have to confirm each week that you are still eligible.
who_it_helps: People laid off or whose employer ran out of work
Workers with enough recent New Jersey wages
People out of work and looking for a job

sources.title: Who is eligible for benefits?
sources.publisher: New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development, Division of Unemployment Insurance
sources.excerpt:
When you first apply for Unemployment Insurance benefits, we look at a few different factors to see if you qualify.
Unemployment benefits are based on wage information from your employers in the last 18 months. If you live in NJ but only worked in other states, you should apply in a state where you physically worked.
We need to know why you're out of work, and whether your recent earnings meet the minimum required by law.
After you first qualify for benefits, you will need to meet some additional requirements in order to keep receiving them.
Some workers, like school employees and business owners, have their own unique qualifications. If you are self-employed and do not pay for Unemployment Insurance through your paycheck, you may not be eligible for benefits.
Read our FAQs on who is eligible for benefits here .
Why are you unemployed?
Unemployment Insurance benefits are meant for people who lose their job “through no fault of their own,” such as an employer’s lack of work or a layoff due to downsizing. If you voluntarily quit your job for reasons that were not work-related, or you were terminated for misconduct, your eligibility will need to be reviewed. A representative from our division (a claims examiner) will conduct a fact-finding interview by either phone or email to determine whether you are eligible for Unemployment Insurance benefits. Your employer(s) may also be requested to participate. The claims examiner will review the facts that you and your employer(s) provide, and determine your eligibility based on the law.
If you were fired due to misconduct or you quit voluntarily, your benefits may be delayed or denied.
Read more about quitting or getting fired.
Did you earn enough during your "base year period" of employment?
To qualify for unemployment payments from New Jersey, you must have made at least a certain amount of money during your "base year." You don’t have to calculate your weekly benefit rate. Department of Labor staff will do these calculations when they review your application.
Your weekly payment amount is determined by the earnings you made in your base year.
Minimum earnings
If you applied in 2025 : You must have earned at least $303 per week for 20 or more weeks in covered employment during your base year, or a total of at least $15,200.
If you're applying in 2026: You must have earned at least $310 per week for 20 or more weeks in covered employment during your base year, or a total of at least $15,500.
